title: The Lost Art of the Handwritten Note
author: Admired Leadership
summary: A defence of an obsolete medium on the grounds that its inefficiency is the message. The author opens by ruling out the alternatives — email fails to carry certain messages and the greeting card scores badly on authenticity — and proposes the handwritten note as the remedy for comfort, gratitude, congratulations, condolence and encouragement alike. The argument for its power is that words in one's own hand signal the recipient is worth the time and effort, producing an impression no other medium replicates and an object people save and reread for years. The usual excuse of time is dispatched neatly: the cost is exactly what carries the meaning. The piece then makes its real diagnosis, which is not logistical but psychological — what actually stops people is perfectionism, the search for the right words, and the fear of falling short of what they feel. The author calls this self-regard rather than modesty, and argues that withholding imperfect words robs others of encouragement they could have used. The closing instruction is characteristically concrete: go buy stationery.
points: The author converts the standard objection into the argument — the time a note takes is more than half of what it communicates, so efficiency would destroy the medium.
The real obstacle is identified as the need for perfection rather than scarcity of time, which relocates the problem from the calendar to the writer's insecurity.
Perfectionism is reframed as selfishness: fretting over the right words is described as thinking more about oneself than about the person who would have received them.
Durability is offered as proof of effect — the recipient keeps and rereads the note for years, which the author treats as the definition of a treasure.
The same medium is claimed to serve a wide emotional range, from condolence to congratulation, without the tonal failures of email or a printed card.
quotes: There are times when email simply does not convey the message we want to send. And the Hallmark card falls woefully short on the authenticity scale.
Whether you’re writing to offer comfort, gratitude, congratulations, condolences, or encouragement, handwritten notes create a connection between people that is hard to replicate.
A single note can leave an indelible mark, one where the receiver saves and rereads the note for years to come.
That the other party deserves the time and energy it takes you is more than half the message.
Actually, what prevents most people from writing handwritten notes is not time, however, but the need for perfection.
Handwritten notes are a lost art because we think more about ourselves than others.
